# Introduction

A **task** is an instructed activity: a set of goals to be achieved or a set of actions
to be performed, or a combination of these, under conditions the experimenter controls,
so that what participants do can be attributed to the mental processes the task was
designed to engage.

HED task models describe tasks in terms that are the same for every task. This page
says why that is needed and gives a short account of the two models; the pages that
follow give each in full.

## Why model tasks

Experiments in cognitive and behavioral neuroscience are built from tasks, but the
datasets they produce rarely say what the task was in a form a machine can act on. A
data repository knows what files a dataset contains, and usually knows the task only as
a free-text label such as `task-flanker` or `task-rest`. Three things follow.

- **A name does not say what was done.** Two laboratories that both ran "a Stroop task"
  may have asked for a spoken color name or a key press, used words or faces, and paid
  the participant or not. The name hides the differences that matter for comparing the
  mental processes associated with the data.
- **The same task goes by different names**, and a search for one name misses the
  others.
- **Different tasks share a great deal**, and nothing records it. A flanker task and a
  Stroop task are the same kind of game with one rule answered differently; a named
  task tells a reader nothing about that.

A model answers the same questions about every task. Two tasks can then be compared
answer by answer, datasets can be searched by what the participant did and not only by
what the task was called, and a task that has no standard name can still be described.

## The task model in brief

Every task is modeled as a **game** that the participant, the player, is asked to play.
A game is described by five things.

| Part | The question it answers | Example: the Stroop Color-Word Task |
|---|---|---|
| Game type | What kind of game is the player playing? | Respond under a rule |
| Game rules | How is this game played? | An irrelevant dimension, the word, competes with the correct response |
| Game motivators | Why does the player try? | Instructions only; nothing is won or lost |
| Game phases | Does the game have parts beyond its own structure? | None |
| Game facets | How is the game delivered? | Visual words on a computer screen, answered aloud into a microphone, in fixed-time trials |

There are ten game types. Each game type has its own rule questions, and every rule
has a default answer, so a model states only the answers that differ. The motivators,
phases and facets are the same questions for every game type. Every answer comes from
a closed [game vocabulary](tasks/vocabulary.md), and each facet value corresponds to
HED tags.

A model also names the settings a study chooses (a retention interval, a set size),
describes the material in a sentence, and records any second game played with the
first, such as fixation held throughout. [The task model](task_model.md) gives all of
this in full, with worked examples.

## The cognitive process model in brief

A **cognitive process** is a mental operation hypothesized to occur during a trial,
such as response inhibition, working memory updating or reward anticipation. The
process model is a list of {{ n_processes }} standard processes in {{ n_categories }}
categories, each with a definition and references.

A task is **linked** to the processes it is hypothesized to engage: the Stroop
Color-Word Task to interference control, selective attention, conflict monitoring and
three more. A link is a hypothesis recorded from the literature, not a measurement.
The two models answer different questions about a task, what the participant does and
what that is thought to engage, and they are kept apart so that the first does not
depend on the second. [The cognitive process model](process_model.md) gives the detail.

## The task catalog

The models are developed on a **task catalog** of {{ n_tasks }} traditional tasks: the
named paradigms of the field, such as the Stroop Color-Word Task, the N-Back Task and
the Iowa Gambling Task. Each task in the catalog has

- a canonical name, its aliases, a definition and a description;
- a **game model** of its standard form, in the five parts above;
- an **inclusion test**, three lists (procedure, manipulations, measurements) that
  decide whether a particular experiment is an instance of the task;
- its **variants**, the other forms of the task that whole studies run, each stating
  only how it differs from the standard form;
- its links to **cognitive processes**; and
- references, and the corresponding Cognitive Atlas entry where there is one.

Tasks are filed under {{ n_families }} **task families** (conflict and interference
tasks, recall and recognition tests, and so on) for browsing. A family is a browsing
aid; the game type is the classification.

```{include} _generated/counts_table.md
```

The catalog is the starting point, not the goal. Traditional tasks were modeled first
because they are well documented and widely used, and modeling them is what produced
the vocabulary. The tasks of individual papers and datasets are modeled next, in the
same terms; [The modeling process](modeling_process.md) describes how, and the template
used for a paper.

## Where the catalog came from

The starting corpus was the [Cognitive Atlas](https://www.cognitiveatlas.org/), a
community-built ontology of cognitive concepts and the tasks that measure them. Its
task list was narrowed to paradigms that produce event-structured data, its concepts
were reshaped into processes that can be placed in a trial, and a gap analysis added
paradigms the Atlas never registered. Every task and process is mapped back to the
Atlas entry by entry. The pages under Related resources describe the
[Cognitive Atlas](atlas/what_is_the_cognitive_atlas.md), say how the
[catalog and the Atlas differ](atlas/the_catalog_vs_the_atlas.md), and compare the
catalog with [CogPO](cogpo/the_catalog_vs_cogpo.md), the Cognitive Paradigm Ontology;
those pages call the task catalog and its process list "the Catalog".

## Task models and HED

HED annotates what actually happened in an experiment, event by event, with a time for
each: the onset of the word RED printed in blue, 2.35 s into the run. A task model
describes the design those events belong to, once for the whole run: what the
participant was asked to do and under what rules. The two meet in the game facets,
whose values carry the HED tags that express them. How a task model will be carried in
HED annotations and in dataset metadata is not yet decided; the identifiers here are
working identifiers and are not
[HED schema terms](https://www.hedtags.org/hed-resources/HedSchemas.html).

## Identifiers

Every entity has a typed identifier, so an identifier met anywhere can be classified
at sight:

| Kind | Form | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task | `hedtsk_<slug>` | `hedtsk_stroop_color_word` |
| Task variant | `hedvar_<task slug>__<variant slug>` | `hedvar_stroop_color_word__counting_stroop` |
| Process | `hed_<slug>` | `hed_response_inhibition` |
| Process category | `<slug>` | `inhibitory_control_and_conflict_monitoring` |
| Task family | `<slug>` | `conflict_and_interference` |
| Game type, rule, motivator, phase, facet and their values | `<slug>` | `respond_to_rule`, `irrelevant_dimension` |

The `hed_` prefix on process identifiers is a working prefix and is not a claim of HED
schema membership. Identifiers are provisional while the models are being developed;
when they stabilize, renames will become aliases.
